title: Lesson 33: Bulkification & Trigger Frameworks: Limits-Aware Design That Scales
description: Why a trigger that works on one record fails on a data load, and how bulkification plus a trigger framework keep every layer working on collections under the governor ceiling.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Bulkification & Trigger Frameworks: Limits-Aware Design That Scales”, a Bulk API load of 1,000 records hits an object whose trigger is already written for collections. How many times does the trigger execute, and why is each execution safe?
options: Once, because a single DML statement is one transaction with one governor budget.
Five times, because triggers batch at 200 records and each firing is a fresh transaction with its own governor budget.
Two hundred times, once per record, with the budget resetting on every firing.
Once per record, but all the firings share one governor budget.
questions.explanation: Triggers operate on batches of 200 records, so 1,000 records fire the trigger five times, and the design target is the spend inside one firing, not the spend across the load.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: SOQL or DML inside a per-record loop makes resource use scale with batch size while the governor budget does not, so the query moves to an IN :Trigger.new bind and the DML becomes one call on a collected list.
A trigger that reads Trigger.new[0] is acceptable as long as the user interface usually saves one record at a time.
DML inside a loop is safe because each update call is cheap, and only SOQL counts against the statement budget.
Wrapping each record’s work in its own savepoint and rollback keeps a looped trigger inside its governor limits.
questions.explanation: Bulking the query and the DML into one call each makes consumption grow with the number of distinct objects touched rather than the number of records.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Multiple triggers on one object are preferable because each one stays small and readable.
All of an object’s rules, DML, and validation should live in the trigger file so the logic is easy to find.
One thin trigger per object that routes to handler and service classes restores ordered execution and stops redundant queries from sharing the same governor budget.
A recursion guard becomes unnecessary once bulkification is done, because triggers batch at 200 records anyway.
questions.explanation: A single entry point per object keeps the firing order explicit, keeps one budget in view, and moves the logic into classes that a unit test can call directly.
